etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Possibly from Old Japanese; first attested in the 新撰字鏡 (Shinsen Jikyō, “Newly Compiled Mirror of Characters”) of 898­­­–901 CE.
Appears to be derived as the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb あくぶ (akubu), although this verb form isn't attested until the 枕草子 (Makura Sōshi, “The Pillow Book”) of 1002.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese verb す (su, “to do”), from Proto-Japonic *su. Cognate with Okinawan すん (sun).
As with all verbs, during the Middle Japanese stage in the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, the 終止形 (shūshikei, “terminal or sentence-ending form”) was gradually lost as the 連体形 (rentaikei, “attributive form”) came to be used for both the attributive and terminal grammatical roles, realigning the conjugations.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 主人 (MC tsyuX nyin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 任す (makasu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Short for 一(いっ)個(こ)人(じん) (ikkojin) or 各(かく)個(こ)人(じん) (kakukojin), from 一(いっ)個(こ)の人(ひと) (ikko no hito), a calque of English individual.
Listed in the 1912 work 英独仏和哲学字彙 (Ei-Doku-Futsu-Wa Tetsugaku Jii, “Dictionary of English, German, and French Philosophical Terms”) as a translation of English individual.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki₁zu⟩ → */kizu/ → /kizu/
From Old Japanese 瑕 (ki₁zu).
Any apparent relation to verb 切(き)る (kiru, “to cut”) is rejected by mid-vowel preservation of its Ryukyuan cognates.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sjau/ → /sʲɔː/ → /sʲoː/
From Middle Chinese 傷 (MC syang).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 劇 /剧.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Pronounced かくむ (kakumu) in the Nara period (奈(な)良(ら)時(じ)代(だい) (Nara jidai), 710–794 CE), it was alternately pronounced かこむ (kakomu) since the middle of the Heian period (平(へい)安(あん)時(じ)代(だい) (Heian jidai), 794–1185 CE). The shift to かこむ (kakomu) is likely due to influence from the verb 囲(かこ)う (kakou), of similar meaning.
An alternate pronunciation かごむ (kagomu), with the medial /k/ becoming voiced to /g/, was formerly widely used, as recorded in the 史記抄(しきしょう) (shikishō) written in the Muromachi period (室(むろ)町(まち)時(じ)代(だい) (Muromachi jidai), c. 1336–1573).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Noun senses are attested from the 8th century, with suffix use later. See 形(かた) (kata). Compare also 姿(すがた) (sugata, “appearance, likeness”), 模(かたぎ) (katagi, “model, pattern, template”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 大学(だいがく) (daigaku) + 院(いん) (-in)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 端 (tsuma, “side, edge”), indicating the person who is at the side of someone: a spouse. Compare the English expression better half.
This term originally referred to either a male (husband) or female (wife) spouse. In modern usage, this term refers only to a female spouse.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: By extension from the at the side sense.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 妻 (MC tshej|tshejH, “wife”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 娯 (ご, go), enjoyment + 楽 (らく, raku), comfort

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 害 (hajᴴ, “injury”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 広(ひろ) (hiro, stem of 広(ひろ)い (hiroi, “wide; open”)) + 場(ば) (ba, “place”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From interjection あや (aya, “oh”) + しい (-shii).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Previously declined as an upper bigrade verb, but then became quadrigrade by the Edo period, where it would also rarely conjugate as a monograde verb.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 教(おし)える (oshieru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/jɨau/ → /jɔː/ → /joː/
From Middle Chinese 樣 (MC yangH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the continuative form of 疲れる (tsukareru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 立(た)つ (tatsu, “to stand”) + 止(と)まる (tomaru, “to stop”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *suntuy ~ *sunti.
Possibly a compound of す (*su, unknown, possibly the same source as 脛(すね) (sune, “shin”)) + 霊(ち), 血(ち), 乳(ち) (chi, “life essence, spirit, power; blood; milk”), with the chi changing to ji due to rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 策 (tsrheak).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 赤(あか)し (akashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Cognate with 明るい (akarui, “bright”).
Medial voiceless plosives, like /-k-/, underwent voicing, then spirantization, then gliding, then being dropped, before /-i, -u, -e, -o/. As this intervocalic sound-change did not occur before /-a/(Hamano, 2000), Middle Japanese /akaki/ became /akai/ 赤い.
⟨akaki₁⟩ → */akakʲi/ → */akaɡʲi/ → */akaɣi/ → */akaji/ → */akai/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *əkəru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 越ゆ (ko₁yu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *koyai-.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 足(あ) (a, “foot”) + 所(と) (to, “place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 跡 (MC tsjek).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Aphesis of 跡(あと) (ato).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally kakayaku. Samuel Martin suggests the initial kaka- element is a mimetic word. The -yaku element may be the verb-forming suffix やく (-yaku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wa.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 追(お)う (ou, “to chase”) + 付(つ)く (tsuku)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 錆び (sabi), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 錆(さ)びる (sabiru, “to rust”, intransitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Wasei kango from elements 魅(み) (mi, “charm, allure, fascination”) + 力(りょく) (-ryoku, “power”).
First attested in 1911 in Jun'ichirō Tanizaki's short story 秘密(ひみつ) (Himitsu, “The Secret”) (see quotation).
